steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The fix for the definition problem is to define medieval epistemology as "the epistemological beliefs of the medieval epistemologists." The historian claims this definition will finally tell us what does and does not belong in medieval epistemology.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
Historians have failed to produce a definition that settles what belongs in medieval epistemology.

With the new definition, the test for any epistemological claim is simple: did any medieval epistemologist believe it? If one did, the claim is in. If one believed the opposite, the opposite claim is in too.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The test has one input: a list of the medieval epistemologists. Everything depends on having that list. How would we know who belongs on it? Presumably they are the thinkers who did medieval epistemology. But that is the very thing we are trying to define.

So given that the definition sounds tidy, how could we argue it still fails to settle what is included? Show that we cannot agree on who the medieval epistemologists were. Then the test has nothing to run on.

Notice what is NOT a problem for the historian: disagreement. The historian already says that if one epistemologist believed X and another believed the opposite, both claims count. Contradictions among the epistemologists were built into the plan.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer that makes it hard to identify who the medieval epistemologists were. If we can't pick them out, the definition can't tell us what is included.

Watch out for answers about epistemologists contradicting each other. The historian built that into the plan, so it doesn't weaken it.

notes.body: Overlap with ancient thinkers doesn't stop the test from running. Ask the historian's question about a shared belief: did any medieval epistemologist believe it? Yes, so it is in. Where else the belief came from has no effect on whether the definition can sort claims.

This is about why they held their epistemological beliefs, not which beliefs they held. The definition only asks whether a medieval epistemologist believed a claim. A belief shaped by "nonepistemological matters" is still one of their epistemological beliefs, and the test still sorts it.

The definition only collects their "epistemological beliefs," and the historian only asks about "some epistemological claim." Passages that are "clearly not about epistemology" are simply left out. Mixed writings make the reading longer, but they don't stop the test from deciding what is included.

This is the trap the stimulus warned us about. The historian says that if any medieval epistemologists believed the opposite of a claim, that opposite claim also counts. Contradictions were planned for, so this answer describes something the definition already handles. It doesn't make the definition any harder to apply.

The definition sorts claims by asking whether "any medieval epistemologists" believed them. That test needs an agreed list of who the epistemologists were. If there is "much debate" about which thinkers, "if any," qualify, the test can't run, and the definition fails to settle what is included, which was the whole problem it promised to solve. The move to repeat: when a definition leans on a group, attack our ability to identify that group.

why: Evidence step misstated the rule (said an opposite belief means epistemology 'did not believe X'), Evaluate/Goal used gendered pronouns, and the choice notes were long, em-dash heavy and partly padded; known_problem was stale since Goal already pointed away from D.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The fact that some crops are being genetically engineered to produce important drugs raises the possibility that these drugs will end up in the general food supply.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into a nearby field of ordinary crops of the same species, the pollen could fertilize that ordinary crop and turn it into a drug-producing crop.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
The consumer advocate's worry is a chain of links:

drug crop → pollen drifts into a nearby field of the same species
pollen fertilizes the ordinary crop → ordinary crop becomes drug-producing
drug-producing crop is harvested for food → drug ends up in the food supply

The stimulus gives evidence for the first two links. The last link is assumed. A plant that produces a drug somewhere in its tissue is not the same as a drug in the food we take from that plant.

Given that the pollen could convert a neighboring crop, how could we argue the drug still won't reach the food supply? Show that the converted crop's food part wouldn't carry the drug.

Also notice how mild the conclusion is: it only says the development "raises the possibility" of drugs in the food supply. To weaken it, an answer has to cut a link in the chain. Making the outcome less harmful, less widespread, or easier to deal with afterward leaves the possibility standing.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
Look for an answer that breaks a link in the chain, most likely the last one: even if an ordinary crop turns into a drug-producing crop, the drug never gets into the food.

Skip answers about how dangerous the drugs are, how much of the food supply is involved, or what we could do after contamination. None of those touch whether the drugs could get in.

notes.body: This lowers the stakes, not the chance. The conclusion is only that the drugs might "end up in the general food supply." Harmless drugs in our food are still drugs in our food, so the possibility the advocate raised is untouched.

This is a conditional, and the condition is never met. It says no drift means no risk, but nothing tells us drift is actually being prevented. If anything, it confirms that drift is the route to contamination, which is the advocate's own story.

Smaller crops are still part of the food supply. The advocate never claimed the drugs would reach the biggest crops, only that they could end up in "the general food supply." Shrinking how much food is involved doesn't break any link in the chain.

This breaks the last link. Grant everything the advocate says: the pollen drifts, fertilizes the ordinary crop, and turns it into a drug-producing crop. The drugs are still "not present in any part of the plant used for food," so harvesting that crop for food puts no drug into the food supply. The move to repeat: map the chain from cause to feared result, then find the answer that blocks a link the author never supported.

Being able to identify a converted crop is not the same as keeping it out of the food supply. To make this weaken, we'd have to add that identified crops are always pulled before harvest, and the answer never says that. As written, the drug could still get into food.

why: Evaluate was a rambling first-person list of speculations with a gendered pronoun and never isolated the unsupported last link; notes were long, em-dash heavy, and E claimed detection supports the argument's premise.
